In 1985, a gallon of gas cost about a dollar. Nobody had a cell phone. And at Costco, a hot dog and a soda cost one dollar and fifty cents.
Today, gas costs three times as much. Your phone costs more than your first car. And the Costco hot dog? Still a dollar fifty.
Adjusted for inflation, that combo should cost more than four dollars. Costco sells around 245 million of them a year. Its own executives have admitted the deal loses money.
So how does a company that refuses to make money on its most famous product end up earning more than nine billion dollars in a single year? The answer is hiding in plain sight. And once you see it, you'll never look at a Costco receipt the same way again.

Costco opened its first warehouse in Seattle in 1983. Two years later, it started selling hot dogs from a simple cart outside a store in Portland, Oregon. The price was a dollar fifty, soda included.
That number became part of the company's identity. By the 2010s, food and beef prices had climbed for decades. The hot dog was losing money.
So Craig Jelinek, who would later become Costco's CEO, went to co-founder Jim Sinegal with a simple idea: raise the price. Maybe to a dollar seventy-five.
Sinegal's answer has become business legend. He told him: "If you raise the effing hot dog, I will kill you. Figure it out."
It was a joke, of course. But it was also an order. The hot dog would not change. The company would have to change around it.

For years, Costco bought its hot dogs from an outside brand. In 2009, it switched to its own Kirkland Signature hot dogs and started making them itself.
Today Costco runs its own hot dog production. It controls the meat, the factory and the trucks. Every middleman it removes is a cost it no longer pays. That is how a price from 1985 survives in 2026.
But here's the thing. Even with all that work, the hot dog was never meant to be a big moneymaker. It was meant to do something else. And to understand what, we need to talk about a chicken.

Costco has sold its rotisserie chicken for four ninety-nine since around the year 2000. Competitors raised their prices. Costco didn't.
In a 2015 earnings call, Costco's chief financial officer admitted the company was giving up 30 to 40 million dollars a year in margin just to keep that price. Then, in 2019, Costco went further. It opened a 450 million dollar poultry complex in Nebraska that can process around two million chickens a week.
Why go through all that trouble for a five dollar bird? Look at where the chickens are in the store. They're almost always at the very back.
To get one, you walk past the TVs, the jewelry, the giant jars of nuts and the wine. Very few people buy only the chicken and leave. Last year Costco sold about 157 million of them. Each one is a reason to walk through the whole store.
Retailers call this a loss leader. The hot dog and the chicken aren't products. They're bait.

But loss leaders alone don't explain Costco. Lots of stores have cheap items to get you in the door. Then they make it back on everything else.
Costco plays a different game. It has a rule that goes back to its founders. No brand-name item can be marked up more than 14% over what Costco paid for it. For its own Kirkland Signature products, the limit is 15%.
That sounds like a lot until you compare it. Many grocery stores mark items up by 25% or more. Some department stores mark up by 50% or even double.
So Costco's overall gross margin sits around 11% of sales. For every hundred dollars you spend there, Costco keeps about eleven dollars before paying rent, staff, electricity and everything else. That is razor thin.
And Kirkland Signature is a big part of how that works. Because Costco doesn't pay for big ad campaigns for its own brand, it can sell Kirkland products for less and still make its margin. Kirkland now sells around 86 billion dollars a year, more than many of the biggest consumer brands in the world.
So if Costco barely profits from what it sells, where does nine billion dollars of profit come from?

The answer is in your wallet. It's the membership card.
To shop at Costco, you pay a yearly fee. In the U.S., a basic Gold Star membership costs 65 dollars. An Executive membership costs 130 dollars.
Now look at the numbers. In fiscal year 2026, Costco brought in about 303 billion dollars in revenue. Almost all of that came from selling stuff. But about 5.9 billion dollars came from membership fees.
That same year, Costco's total profit was about 9.2 billion dollars.
Read that again. Membership fees alone were equal to almost two thirds of Costco's entire profit. And those fees cost Costco almost nothing to collect. There is no product to buy, no shelf to stock, no truck to send.
This is the real secret. Costco isn't really a store that sells you things. It's a club that sells you access. The products are kept as cheap as possible so the membership feels like a bargain. And the membership is where the money is.

A membership business only works if people come back. And Costco members do.
Costco has about 84 million paid members worldwide. Around 90% of them renew every year. In the U.S. and Canada, the rate is even higher.
Think about how rare that is. Most gyms, apps and streaming services would love to keep nine out of ten customers every single year.
And the most loyal members are the ones paying the most. Executive members get 2% back on most purchases, so they spend more to earn more back. They account for roughly three quarters of all Costco sales.
Every hot dog, every cheap chicken, every low price on a TV makes that card feel worth it. Then the renewal comes, and people pay again without a second thought.

Put it all together and you get what business people call a flywheel.
Low prices attract members. More members means Costco buys in enormous volumes. Huge volumes give Costco the power to demand lower prices from suppliers. Lower costs mean even lower prices. And lower prices attract even more members.
Costco also pays its warehouse workers well by retail standards, around 31 dollars an hour on average in the U.S. Happier workers stay longer, which means less training and better service. That's one more piece of the machine.
Every turn of the wheel makes the next turn easier. And it all started with a promise that sounds almost silly: never raise the price of the hot dog.

So, does Costco lose money on its dollar fifty hot dog? Maybe. But that's the wrong question.
The right question is: how much would Costco lose if it raised the price? It would lose the story, the trust and the reason millions of people renew their card every year.
The cheapest thing in the store might be the most valuable thing Costco owns.
